intros.market: Internet Security Research Group commands 38.5% of certificate issuance, followed by Google Trust Services at 20.7% and DigiCert at 14.7%. The top three CAs control 73.9% of issuance (CR3), while the top five account for 91.6% (CR5). The HHI of 2307 indicates a highly concentrated market, yet 89 CAs remain trusted across the ecosystem, with 75 operating in the long tail below the top five.
intros.trust: 335 total roots are distributed across four trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four programs and just 38 CA owners hold trust in all stores simultaneously. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating significant store disagreement that complicates chain validation and operational planning. This fragmentation means a certificate chain trusted in Edge may fail in Chrome or Safari, forcing CAs to maintain multiple hierarchies and increasing the attack surface administrators must monitor.
intros.conc: An HHI of 2307 reflects a market dominated by three CAs controlling nearly three-quarters of all issuance, creating systemic dependency on a handful of operators. If any of the top three CAs experienced a distrust event, the impact would cascade across tens of millions of sites, far exceeding historical incidents. The 89 trusted CAs include a long tail of 75 operators with minimal market share but identical trust store inclusion, amplifying tail risk without diversifying systemic exposure.
intros.tail: 75 CAs operate below the top five with negligible issuance share yet retain full inclusion in browser trust stores, granting them the same privileges as high-volume operators. These low-volume CAs collectively represent 8.4% of issuance but introduce disproportionate risk, as incident rates and governance oversight do not scale with market share. The tail includes operators with fewer resources, less mature compliance programs, and lower visibility, yet a misissuance from any tail CA can affect millions of users.
intros.geo: 91.6% of certificate issuance originates from CAs incorporated in the United States, with 15 US-based CAs dominating global trust. Europe accounts for 8.4% of issuance across 44 CAs, while Asia-Pacific holds just 0.08% despite 17 active CAs. This geographic concentration amplifies jurisdiction risk, as US legal and regulatory frameworks govern nearly all certificate issuance affecting global internet infrastructure.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trust store inclusion, though they account for only 0.07% of issuance. These entities operate under different accountability structures than commercial CAs, with potential exposure to state-directed surveillance or compelled issuance that audits and public oversight may not detect. Their presence in trusted root stores grants them the same technical authority as Let's Encrypt or Google, despite fundamentally different governance models.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high risk for compelled disclosure or surveillance, including China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey represent moderate risk, with legal frameworks that permit government access to cryptographic material or CA operations under national security authorities. Combined with the finding that 91.6% of issuance originates from US-incorporated CAs, the WebPKI faces concentrated exposure to a small number of legal regimes that can compel cooperation without public disclosure.
intros.ops: 1547 total incidents have been recorded across 54 CAs, with misissuance accounting for 602 events and governance failures contributing 495. CAs self-detect only 26% of incidents, while external researchers identify 18% and automated tools catch 17%, leaving root programs to uncover just 4%. Policy failures number 188, disclosure failures 137, and audit findings contributed 107 incidents, suggesting that formal compliance mechanisms catch a minority of operational problems before they escalate.
intros.crypto: Root algorithm distribution, key size compliance, and adherence to cryptographic standards form the foundation of trust store security policies. This tab analyzes the cryptographic posture of trusted roots, identifying aging algorithms, non-compliant key sizes, and roots operating beyond their intended lifespan. Cryptographic weaknesses in root material directly impact the security of all descendant certificates, making this dimension critical to systemic risk assessment.
intros.distrust: 16 distrust events have occurred across the ecosystem, with 14 involving compliance or operational failures and 10 following a pattern of repeated issues. Negligent noncompliance accounts for 7 posture classifications, while willful circumvention led to 3 events and demonstrated incompetence contributed 3 more. The median runway from distrust announcement to effective date spans 1185 days, giving distrusted CAs over three years to wind down operations, far longer than the 47-day certificate validity ceiling planned for 2029.
intros.policy: Certificate Authority Browser Forum members number 56, but only 21 contribute actively, leaving 35 organizations with zero participation in ballot processes or governance work. Stephen Davidson of Sectigo leads individual ballot activity with 36 proposals and 1 endorsement, while Sectigo is the most active organizational contributor. This concentration of policy work among a few actors means the compliance surface that all 89 trusted CAs must navigate is shaped by a small subset of stakeholders, amplifying the influence of active participants while leaving most CAs as passive rule-takers. Meanwhile, the regulatory obligation count has grown 121x since 2000 to 6664 total requirements, with 76% classified as mandatory, yet no ballots have passed since 2022 to streamline or consolidate these demands. 43 active TLS issuers face three upcoming validity ceiling changes under SC-081, with median certificate usage currently at 67 days while 4 CAs remain at risk for the March 2026 200-day threshold and 5 for the March 2027 100-day limit. Only 8 CAs are ready for the March 2029 47-day ceiling, revealing that most CAs have not yet adapted issuance practices to anticipated requirements even as the compliance burden expands across CA/B Forum BRs, root programs, IETF, WebTrust/ETSI, and ISO/NIST standards.
intros.governance: In 2025, Chrome provided substantive oversight on 18.4% of the 223 reported incidents, Mozilla on 9.9%, and Apple on 5.4%, while Microsoft contributed zero oversight activity. This represents a sharp decline from 2019, when Chrome engaged on 67.8% of 255 bugs and Mozilla on 78.0%, suggesting root programs have reduced their incident review activity by more than two-thirds even as the incident corpus has grown to 1832 bugs. The withdrawal of active oversight leaves CAs with less feedback on compliance gaps, potentially explaining the persistence of governance failures and misissuance patterns documented in the operational risk data.
intros.community: 56 organizations hold CA/B Forum membership, but 35 contribute zero ballot activity, leaving 21 members to shape policy for an ecosystem of 89 trusted CAs. Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots, representing concentrated influence over governance decisions that affect all participants. This participation gap means that most trusted CAs operate under rules they did not help draft, while the policy-active minority defines standards, validity periods, and compliance obligations without broad engagement from the operators who must implement them.
intros.audit: Auditors detected just 28% of incidents that occurred during the audit periods they reviewed, meaning 117 of 414 in-scope incidents were caught while 297 appeared in clean audit letters. 37 CAs show high transparency gaps between audit attestations and their Bugzilla incident histories, while 4 CAs received qualified opinions and 11 changed auditors in 2025. WebTrust self-reported findings appear in 58.8% of letters and ETSI self-reports in 66.1%, but these rates indicate that roughly one-third of audit letters contain no self-disclosed issues despite the broader incident corpus. KPMG audits 11 CAs with an average quality score of 73.3 but an average transparency gap of 99.6 days, while the auditor HHI of 526.9 reflects moderate concentration among the top five firms, suggesting limited competitive pressure to improve detection rates.
